items.summary: Decentralized multi-robot shape formation in GPS-denied environments is important for search-and-rescue and disaster response. Conventional consensus-based formation controllers can violate safe separation, oscillate, or stall when communication degrades, sensors are noisy, or an agent drops out. This paper proposes a resilient decentralized controller that combines Huber-weighted consensus and Exponential Moving Average (EMA) state estimation with a Dual-Layer Artificial Potential Field (APF) safety barrier. The first layer adds an anti-symmetric lateral deflection to resolve head-on encounters between peers; the second applies a normal-plus-tangential circulation field around static obstacles. The framework is evaluated on five simulated nonholonomic differential-drive robots in Gazebo Harmonic (ROS 2 Jazzy). Three runs are compared: a linear consensus baseline, the same baseline under faults (15% packet loss, 50-150 ms delay, σ = 0.18 m sensor noise, and a mid-run agent blackout), and the proposed controller under the same faults. The fault-free baseline reached the pentagon fastest (0.0156 m final RMS error) but its minimum separation fell to 0.3918 m, with 31 logged violations of the 0.50 m margin. Under faults the baseline reached 0.0546 m with 5 violations (minimum 0.4833 m). The proposed controller recorded no violations, kept a minimum separation of 0.6757 m, and reached 0.0368 m final error, at the cost of slower convergence (about 21 s versus about 12-15 s). Results are from single simulation runs, and the safety barrier is empirical rather than formally guaranteed.

items.summary: Background. Antireflux fundoplication failure — recurrent reflux, dysphagia, gas-bloat syndrome, secondary to a herniated, slipped, too-tight, disrupted, or twisted valve — remains common, and its endoscopic diagnosis lacks a common, standardized reporting language. Aim. To narratively review existing endoscopic instruments for postoperative antireflux valve assessment, the evidence on their interobserver reliability, and to position an original instrument — the Endoscopic Fundoplication Score (SEF) — within this landscape. Methods. Narrative review, with a targeted search in PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar (last search: 24 September 2026) using the terms “fundoplication,” “endoscopic grading,” “gastroesophageal valve,” “Hill classification,” “antireflux surgery outcome,” “interobserver reliability,” “wrap integrity,” and “hiatal hernia recurrence,” covering literature published between 1996 and 2026 in English or with an English abstract, supplemented by reference-list screening of identified articles. Results. Three major endoscopic instruments were identified — the Hill classification (1996), the Jobe system (2004), and the American Foregut Society (AFS) nomenclature (2025) — alongside a descriptive, non-scored taxonomy of failure types (herniated, slipped, tight, disrupted, twisted). The interobserver reliability studies [1,2] identified in this review for the postoperative setting report low agreement, and a retrospective comparison of endoscopy reports [3] documented major discrepancies between external endoscopists and operating surgeons. The AFS classification of esophagogastric junction integrity achieved substantial agreement on static images (κ=0.65) but only fair agreement under dynamic conditions (κ=0.371), and the postoperative AFS nomenclature has not yet been tested for interobserver reliability. The SEF score, an 11-item composite instrument (0–16 points) applied to a cohort of 178 patients, correlated in preliminary single-centre data with the Hill classification, Los Angeles (LA) esophagitis grade, and the Visick patient-satisfaction score (own data, manuscript submitted for publication), offering a numeric, quantifiable alternative to existing categorical systems. The SEF threshold of ≤10 points, defined in the same cohort, is exploratory. Conclusions. The field of postoperative endoscopic antireflux valve assessment remains fragmented, without an interobserver-reliable consensus standard. The SEF score partially addresses this gap through a numeric structure, with experience-based weights and an exploratory threshold, but requires formal interobserver reliability testing and multicenter validation against the surgical gold standard.

items.summary: NANOROBOT-ENHANCED DIGITAL TWINS OF BRAIN STATE AT THE LIMIT A multiscale, uncertainty-aware research atlas on microrobotic observations, neural inverse problems, active model discrimination and the limits of computational brain twins. This research monograph asks whether additional microscale observations or strictly bounded reversible experiments can distinguish competing neural-state models that explain conventional measurements equally well. The twin is explicitly defined as a versioned scientific belief, not a digital person, a mind reader or a clinically validated instrument. Its objective is not maximum model complexity but improved identifiability, calibrated prediction under new conditions and faithful retention of failed hypotheses. The work develops five layers: multiscale neural and microenvironment state representation; posterior equivalence and prior sensitivity; non-clinical safe experimental design; frozen-version forking, rollback and reference ancestry; and blind prospective validation against classical state-space systems and independently specified alternatives. Its research architecture includes 30 distinct mathematical derivation plates linked to later chapters, 82 chapters with five independently paginated research sections apiece, 200 detailed Research Gates and 33 revisable Phoenix Answer Embryos. A DOI evidence ledger identifies existing support for brain modeling, latent neural dynamics, experiment design and preclinical microrobot tracking while preventing those sources from being mistaken for evidence of the proposed integrated system. Key research questions include: Can two equally accurate virtual brains be separated by a small, permissible observation? How can the effect of a measurement itself be separated from neural change? When does a prior dominate the inferred brain state? Can the model predict unseen function rather than reconstruct a training signal? Can another laboratory reproduce a rejected twin and safely return to an earlier version? SCIENTIFIC STATUS AND LIMITATIONS This is a forward-looking, non-clinical research synthesis and experimental hypothesis architecture. It provides no personal medical advice, patient-specific interpretations or instruction to deliver neural interventions. Existing murine microrobot tracking and virtual-brain modeling studies do not establish autonomous neural nanorobot readout, human safety, privacy-sensitive mind inference or therapeutic efficacy. Proposed formulas, experiments, research gates and answer embryos are not newly validated biological laws or executed experiments. The work keeps independent safety vetoes, privacy, external reproducibility and explicit model retirement as first-class constraints. Research questions remain open to refutation, correction and reconstruction by future human and AI researchers.

items.summary: Fisher information metric tensors for the 41 held-out SONICOM test subjects, as used in “Evaluating Spatial Discriminability Preservation in HRTF Upsampling Using Fisher Information” (D. Bassett). Code and reproduction instructions: https://github.com/domfrbassett/fisher-rao-hrtf-upsampling What the tensors are At each of the 793 directions of the SONICOM grid, the 2×2 tensor g = JᵀΣ⁻¹J describes how well the auditory cues separate that direction from its neighbours. J is the spatial Jacobian of the cues: Barumerli monaural PGE features, ILD and MaxIACCe-transformed ITD, each fitted with real spherical harmonics. Σ holds the cue noise (σ_mon = 1.25 dB, σ_ILD = 1 dB, σ_ITD = 0.569). All fields are low-pass filtered at 16 kHz before the cues are extracted. The tensor is expressed in a local tangent basis u₁ = a × r, u₂ = r × u₁, where a = z, or y when |r_z| > 0.9, and its units are d′² per rad². Contents metric_tensors.zip has one folder per subject, metric_tensors/subject_####/ , containing 25 files per subject (1,025 in total): reference_metric_tensor.mat : the dense measured HRTF. <METHOD>_N###_metric_tensor.mat : one file per reconstruction. There are six methods: SUpDEq_SH , SUpDEq_MCA , SUpDEq_NN_MCA_6dB (SUpDEq-Natural-MCA in the paper), SUpDEq_Bary_MCA_6dB , RANF and FSP_AE . Each is reconstructed from N = 100, 19, 5 and 3 retained directions. The 164 natural-neighbour and barycentric files at N = 5 and 3 have status “ not_applicable ”. The interpolation is undefined for those masks, so these files carry no tensors. Variables in each file: metricTensor : the tensors at SH order 6 [2×2×793]. familyGram : per-cue-family Gram matrices JᵀJ before noise weighting, at SH orders 4, 6 and 8 [2×2×793×3 families×3 orders]. They let you recompute the tensors with other noise values or SH orders. In reconstruction files only: crossFamilyGram : the unsymmetrised cross terms J_refᵀ J_recon, same layout as familyGram . airmByDirection : the pointwise AIRM discrepancy from the reference. Metadata: coordinates (Cartesian and azimuth/elevation in degrees), cue band, noise values (reference files only), status (“ completed ” or “ not_applicable ”) and, for not-applicable files, a message giving the reason. SHA256SUMS.txt lists a checksum for every file. Format and use The files are MATLAB v7.3 (HDF5), so MATLAB, h5py or any HDF5 reader can open them. Note that h5py reverses MATLAB’s axis order. scripts/fisher_lib.py in the repository reads them and recomputes tensors, AIRM and thresholds from the Gram matrices. To rerun the analysis scripts, unzip into results/evaluation/ so the subject folders sit in results/evaluation/metric_tensors/ . Provenance Produced with run_evaluation("tensors") from the repository above. The values are numerically identical to the tensor files behind results/evaluation/full_evaluation_summary.csv ; this run additionally stores the cross terms. The tensors are derived from the SONICOM HRTF Dataset (Engel et al., J. Audio Eng. Soc. 71(5), 2023, doi:10.17743/jaes.2022.0066). The SONICOM HRTFs are released under the MIT licence. This work develops research begun for the author’s B.Sc. dissertation at Birmingham City University.

items.summary: LONGITUDINAL DEVICE MIGRATION AND MEANING CONTINUITY AT THE LIMIT Device Replacement × Model Bridging × Control Semantics STARLI RESEARCH WORKS | INSTITUTE XXIV | FLAGSHIP 24 Feng Cheng-en 33 × Starli Research Works This research monograph investigates a deceptively difficult question in long-term brain–computer interfaces: when sensors, acquisition electronics, firmware, electrode geometry, or decoding models change, what would justify the claim that a user's task-grounded control meaning has been preserved? Numerical signal alignment alone cannot establish continuity of intention. Two systems may encode different signals while supporting the same functional command, or produce nearly identical latent representations while mapping to incompatible actions. The volume formulates meaning continuity as a conditional, falsifiable engineering and scientific hypothesis. It connects device-specific observation models, neural recording instability, task and action ontologies, paired old/new sensing periods, latent manifold bridging, longitudinal recalibration, calibrated abstention, functional validation, and an accessible right to reject the proposed migration. Its central commitment is that no amount of predictive accuracy can compensate for invalid authorization, an unverified physical reference, or loss of independent control. The research atlas comprises thirty connected mathematical derivations, eighty-two research chapters, and 410 independently paginated chapter sections that examine observables, inverse explanations, discriminating experiments, uncertainty and noncompensable safeguards, and independent requalification. Two hundred detailed Research Gates propose future falsification and handoff programs, while thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos preserve revisable candidate approaches rather than immutable conclusions. A claim-scoped DOI evidence ledger connects the study to published work on neural recording drift, decoder adaptation, manifold alignment, longitudinal neural interfaces, speech BCIs, user preferences, and neurotechnology ethics. The book is designed for both human researchers and future AI research systems. Its formulas, chapter cross-links, DOI anchors, competing models, negative-result requirements, and successor-focused research cards provide structured entry points for independent reconstruction and informed disagreement. The visual presentation combines ivory pages, navy and teal typography, and large gold mathematical plates, while mathematical expressions are also recorded in searchable source notation and a separate Excel reference index. This is a prospective, nonclinical research architecture. It does not report new patient experiments, demonstrate safe autonomous human neurovascular microrobots, establish a universal device-migration system, or claim continuity of private thoughts, consciousness, or personal identity. Scientific benefit remains conditional on explicit task definitions, qualified device evidence, legitimate permissions, external validation, and the successor's freedom to reject a failed bridge. Research question: What should remain invariant when an interface changes, and who has the authority to say that its meaning has changed?

items.summary: Decentralized multi-robot shape formation in GPS-denied environments is important for search-and-rescue and disaster response. Conventional consensus-based formation controllers can violate safe separation, oscillate, or stall when communication degrades, sensors are noisy, or an agent drops out. This paper proposes a resilient decentralized controller that combines Huber-weighted consensus and Exponential Moving Average (EMA) state estimation with a Dual-Layer Artificial Potential Field (APF) safety barrier. The first layer adds an anti-symmetric lateral deflection to resolve head-on encounters between peers; the second applies a normal-plus-tangential circulation field around static obstacles. The framework is evaluated on five simulated nonholonomic differential-drive robots in Gazebo Harmonic (ROS 2 Jazzy). Three runs are compared: a linear consensus baseline, the same baseline under faults (15% packet loss, 50-150 ms delay, σ = 0.18 m sensor noise, and a mid-run agent blackout), and the proposed controller under the same faults. The fault-free baseline reached the pentagon fastest (0.0156 m final RMS error) but its minimum separation fell to 0.3918 m, with 31 logged violations of the 0.50 m margin. Under faults the baseline reached 0.0546 m with 5 violations (minimum 0.4833 m). The proposed controller recorded no violations, kept a minimum separation of 0.6757 m, and reached 0.0368 m final error, at the cost of slower convergence (about 21 s versus about 12-15 s). Results are from single simulation runs, and the safety barrier is empirical rather than formally guaranteed.

This book proposes a rigorous, falsifiable architecture for self-calibrating nano-neural interfaces that must retain the scientific history of every reference and every update. Its central axiom is that self-calibration does not imply self-certification: measurement claims, permission to change, electrode safety and functional benefit demand independent evidence. The first coupling is the existence of physically traceable internal references that can be challenged against electrically and temporally independent standards. The second is a source-aware drift-diagnostic process that distinguishes electronics gain, electrode-tissue transfer, tissue-like surrogate changes, changing source signals and model/feature drift, explicitly recording instances of nonidentifiability. The third is external functional requalification, which can reject an apparently successful update after hidden-domain testing, material or reference replacement, loss of selectivity, missing raw observations, or inability to reproduce the frozen predecessor. This research monograph is divided into seven causal layers and 82 chapters. Five major subsections of each chapter are assigned independent pages, yielding 410 separately paginated technical essays. Thirty gold mathematical derivations are linked from chapter-opening equations to discriminating experiments. items.summary: Four-dimensional beam-matrix reconstruction from quadrupole scans is the standard way to mea- sure cross-plane coupling and the intrinsic emittances that a decoupling section can recover. We show that a scan of a single thin quadrupole, normal or skew and placed anywhere in a linear lattice, determines at most nine of the ten beam-matrix parameters for any number of settings, because each measured second moment is quadratic in the quadrupole strength. The unmeasured direction lies in the x–y cross block and has a closed form in terms of the transfer matrices; for a quadrupole followed by a drift of length L its nonzero entries are Wxpy = Wpxy = 1 and Wpxpy = −2/L. Both projected emittances are therefore measured, but the beam matrices consistent with the data form a line segment along which the smaller intrinsic emittance ranges from zero to slightly above its true value, so a single-knob scan gives only an upper bound on it. A thick quadrupole restores the miss- ing direction only weakly, its singular value scaling approximately as the sixth power of the magnet length. Scanning two independently powered quadrupoles of any type makes the reconstruction well posed without additional hardware.
items.title: Single-knob quadrupole scans do not determine the intrinsic emittances

items.summary: This report establishes an exact conditional mathematical correspondence between a specified two-component phase model and the sine-Gordon equation appearing in a classical string-theory reduction. Developed within the Harmonic Physics Research Programme, the model uses interacting phase components labelled expansion and contraction in the proposed physical interpretation. For a continuum action with a cosine interaction, constant coefficients and equal component propagation speeds, an invertible change of variables separates the dynamics into an exact nonlinear sine-Gordon equation for the normalized relative phase and a free wave equation for the common phase. The interaction potential can also be expressed through the squared magnitude of the difference between two complex phase components. The derivation retains the full nonlinearity, extending the correspondence beyond the small-angle approximation. Direct numerical evolution of the original component fields provides a reproducible check at finite relative-phase amplitude. The reported breather benchmark reaches a peak relative-phase excursion of approximately 2.574 radians, with a maximum sampled error of approximately 6.3 × 10⁻⁹ radians over two oscillation periods. Component amplitudes remain fixed. Interaction-removal and unequal-speed controls document the failure to recover the same target when the specified conditions are changed. The string-theory connection is examined through the Pohlmeyer reduction of classical strings on R_t × S². A separate conventional kink embedding is checked against the local geometric constraints and string equations of motion. The evolved phase breather is not reconstructed as a string. The established result is a conditional correspondence between reduced classical equations; a full physical or quantum equivalence between the proposed phase model and string theory remains unestablished. Version 1.0 includes the standalone report and an accompanying reproducibility archive containing mathematical derivations, executable Python scripts, numerical settings, sampled synthetic data, control results, figures, source provenance, checksum manifests and reproduction instructions. A documented replay of the retained calculation and an AI-assisted computational audit support inspection and reuse of the reported results. items.summary: The Voynich Manuscript exhibits strong statistical regularities, but the distinction between recoverable grammar and recoverable lexical meaning remains unresolved. This study asks how far a progressively frozen, cross-validated analysis can reconstruct the manuscript’s internal word-building system without assigning meanings from illustrations, candidate languages, or post-hoc English paraphrase. Using canonical transcription, protected holdout partitions, alternate-transcription replication, exact host substitutions, and adversarial stopping rules, the analysis recovers a cumulative left-edge morphology, a transferable inventory of 39 surface CORE-0 stem/bodies, reproducible host-by-right-state coupling, a stable K/T referential contrast, and a directed network among powered lexical cores. The 39-core inventory predicts protected-frame combinatorics and content-blind contextual fingerprints out of sample, while attempts to decompose these bodies into a deeper transferable root layer fail. Nine recurring hosts show strongly replicated coupling to EY/EEY/EDY right-edge states, supporting a distributed morphological paradigm rather than independent left- and right-side systems. A 28-node directed CORE network also replicates across canonical calibration, untouched Holdout, and alternate-transcription tests, yielding neutral outbound- and inbound-biased stem classes without requiring part-of-speech or semantic assignments. On the project’s fully constrained 1,609-line benchmark, 12,299 of 12,495 positions are role-naturalizable (98.4314%), leaving 196 opaque positions. This percentage is explicitly a conditional benchmark-maturity statistic, not a measure of literal plaintext recovery or manuscript-wide translation accuracy. Repeated attempts to cross from structural organization to ordinary lexical meaning—including deeper-root induction, topic clustering, functional-neighborhood anchoring, local lexical syntax, illustration matching, source-language fitting, and prospective semantic transfer—fail the project’s promotion criteria. The resulting contribution is therefore a structural decipherment rather than a lexical one: a reproducible grammatical and morphological architecture together with an empirically identified lexical-identifiability ceiling. The work extends, but is distinct from, the earlier controlled-translation release at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22049207.
items.title: Structural Decipherment Without Lexical Recovery: A Cross-Validated Morphological Analysis of the Voynich Manuscript

items.summary: Adaptive modulation and coding (AMC) improves the spectral efficiency of underwater acoustic (UWA) links, but its feedback is inevitably stale: sound propagates slowly, and by the time channel state information (CSI) arrives, the fast time-varying multipath channel has moved on. Predictive link adaptation therefore needs more than a point forecast: it needs a distribution over each candidate action's consequences. We propose PRB-WM, a physics-regularized Beta world model for predictive per-subcarrier link adaptation on real time-varying UWA channels. A persistence-anchored stochastic latent-space dynamics model learns how the channel evolves; a counterfactual outcome head evaluates, for every candidate modulation and coding scheme (MCS), a Beta-binomial distribution of bit errors on shared imagined futures; and a chance-constrained receding-horizon model predictive controller maximizes expected spectral efficiency subject to a bounded probability of violating the bit error rate (BER) target. To the best of our knowledge, PRB-WM is the first world model for UWA communications. In closed-loop replay of six measured sea-trial links from the public UWA Channel Library against a 24-method pool spanning the full methodological spectrum, PRB-WM attains a mean goodput 87% above the strongest baseline, ranks first on all six time-varying links at the longest lookahead, and is the only method whose realized frame risk decreases systematically with lookahead, meeting the BER-violation contract where no baseline does. Ablations confirm that rollout sampling dispersion is essential to the chance constraint and that the physics anchor is necessary for trainability.
items.title: PRB-WM: Physics-Regularized Beta World Models for Predictive Link Adaptation on Real Time-Varying Underwater Acoustic Channels

items.summary: Singing Accompaniment Generation (SAG) is the process of generating instrumental music for a given clean vocal input. However, existing SAG techniques use source-separated vocals as input and overfit to separation artifacts. This creates a critical train-test mismatch, leading to failure on clean, real-world vocal inputs. We introduce AnyAccomp, a framework that resolves this by decoupling accompaniment generation from source-dependent artifacts. AnyAccomp first employs a quantized melodic bottleneck, using a chromagram and a VQ-VAE to extract a discrete and timbre-invariant representation of the core melody. A subsequent flow-matching model then generates the accompaniment conditioned on these robust codes. Experiments show AnyAccomp achieves competitive performance on separated-vocal benchmarks while significantly outperforming baselines on generalization test sets of clean studio vocals and, notably, solo instrumental tracks. This demonstrates a qualitative leap in generalization, enabling robust accompaniment for instruments - a task where existing models completely fail - and paving the way for more versatile music co-creation tools. Demo audio and code: https://anyaccomp.github.io
items.title: AnyAccomp: Generalizable Accompaniment Generation via Quantized Melodic Bottleneck

items.summary: Image harmonization methods adjust the colour and lighting of an object pasted into a photograph so that it looks native to its new scene, and they are ranked by average error on one benchmark whose test images are real photographs with one object recoloured. One photograph can yield several such test images, and the benchmark promises that no photograph appears in both the training and the test split. We find that 1,399 photographs do, and the composites built on them are a quarter of the test set. Duplicate checks over file names or bytes miss this, because every composite is a different file. On that quarter the three methods we score end to end read two to five times lower error than on the rest, but most of the gap is composition rather than the sharing: the shared composites come almost entirely from one of the benchmark's four source collections, and inside that collection the gap falls to about one and a half times. An official score is therefore an average over two populations, mixed in a proportion the benchmark does not report. We release a test list of 5,581 composites whose construction identities do not appear in training, with four near-duplicate pairs disclosed rather than removed, adoptable without retraining at the price of one rescore per checkpoint. We leave open whether the sharing itself changes what a model learns. Contents of this record. The paper, the supplement, the LaTeX source of both, the record metadata and the licence statement. The identity matcher, the composite-locality and sensitivity checks, the CPU tests, the official iHarmony4 lists and the corrected test list are released under the MIT license at https://github.com/Buljic/only-means-only . What this record does not contain. No dataset, no images, no masks, no model checkpoints and no third-party baseline code or weights; those are described and cited by the paper and remain under their own terms. This is a preprint. items.summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are fast becoming a general interface to sound, yet how far their broad pretraining carries into specialized domains remains largely open. Vessel monitoring, maritime safety, and ocean sensing all depend on recognizing underwater signals, but to our knowledge LALMs have not been systematically evaluated on them. Annotated recordings are costly to collect, and a faithful synthetic alternative has to bring together many interacting factors: the structure of detection pulses, communication waveforms, and ship-radiated noise, and the sound-speed profile, geometry, and multipath propagation through which each reaches the receiver. We address this by proposing \textbf{UA-Bench}, to our knowledge the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating LALMs on underwater acoustic signal recognition. It comprises 375,051 audio records that couple parameterized sources with modeled propagation, so that every record can be traced to the conditions that produced it. The records span these three signal families, and each carries a three-level label hierarchy (13 leaf classes), a templated multi-turn dialogue, and source and channel metadata. We evaluate on a balanced 2,600-record subset with a gated coarse-to-fine protocol that locates each error at source routing, fine-grained classification, or output format, and add a paired silent-audio control to test whether the waveform is actually used. Nine open LALMs, evaluated without task-specific adaptation, reach only 2.0\%--13.1\% leaf accuracy, against a random reference of 7.7\%. The waveform helps source routing far more than leaf recognition (for one model, +29.5 versus +2.3 points over silence), and just four models gain reliably at the leaf level, by at most 4.7 points. UA-Bench thus gives a reference point for these models, and its released training partition supports follow-up adaptation work.

items.summary: This archive is provided as artifact material for the article "Synthesis and Verification of Register Automata over Data Sequences" for SETTA 2026. Abstract: Data sequences, such as time series, traces, and sensor streams, are words over large or infinite data domains. Their properties often depend on comparisons between values at different positions, which finite automata cannot express directly. We study synthesis and verification for Deterministic Register Automata (DRAs) over ordered data sequences. DRAs combine finite control with registers for remembered data values, providing compact symbolic descriptions of quantitative sequence languages. Our technical core is a local-search synthesis procedure and an exact robustness checker for DRAs. We fix the alphabet theory to ordered rationals $(\Q;<,=)$ with rational guard constants and use non-negative affine accumulator costs. For a fixed number of DRA registers, the checker runs in polynomial time; its dependence on that number is exponential. It reduces robustness to coverability and then to a shortest-path problem. Since the search ranges over $\Q^+$, it produces variable-length witnesses and, for RAA-definable alignment costs such as DTW, explores a counterexample space with no a priori length bound. As an application, we use learned DRAs as interpretable surrogates for queried neural sequence classifiers. A probably approximately correct (PAC) validation loop refines rejected candidates, returns genuine non-robustness witnesses for the classifier when found, and accepts a surrogate only with statistical guarantees for fidelity and local stability. We implement the framework in \textit{RAExc}, enabling the synthesis of interpretable automata and the verification of their robustness. We evaluate the approach on benchmark languages and sequentialized MNIST, demonstrating high accuracy while verifying the robustness of the learned automata.

items.summary: This report establishes an exact conditional mathematical correspondence between a specified two-component phase model and the sine-Gordon equation appearing in a classical string-theory reduction. Developed within the Harmonic Physics Research Programme, the model uses interacting phase components labelled expansion and contraction in the proposed physical interpretation. For a continuum action with a cosine interaction, constant coefficients and equal component propagation speeds, an invertible change of variables separates the dynamics into an exact nonlinear sine-Gordon equation for the normalized relative phase and a free wave equation for the common phase. The interaction potential can also be expressed through the squared magnitude of the difference between two complex phase components. The derivation retains the full nonlinearity, extending the correspondence beyond the small-angle approximation. Direct numerical evolution of the original component fields provides a reproducible check at finite relative-phase amplitude. The reported breather benchmark reaches a peak relative-phase excursion of approximately 2.574 radians, with a maximum sampled error of approximately 6.3 × 10⁻⁹ radians over two oscillation periods. Component amplitudes remain fixed. Interaction-removal and unequal-speed controls document the failure to recover the same target when the specified conditions are changed. The string-theory connection is examined through the Pohlmeyer reduction of classical strings on R_t × S². A separate conventional kink embedding is checked against the local geometric constraints and string equations of motion. The evolved phase breather is not reconstructed as a string. The established result is a conditional correspondence between reduced classical equations; a full physical or quantum equivalence between the proposed phase model and string theory remains unestablished. Version 1.0 includes the standalone report and an accompanying reproducibility archive containing mathematical derivations, executable Python scripts, numerical settings, sampled synthetic data, control results, figures, source provenance, checksum manifests and reproduction instructions. A documented replay of the retained calculation and an AI-assisted computational audit support inspection and reuse of the reported results. items.summary: Version 2.0 is a substantive revision of version 1.0 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19174862). It supersedes the earlier procedural interpretation and its exclusion of competing explanations. The revised title is Structural Organization and Interpretive Limits of the Phaistos Disc. Reproduced descriptive findings are retained; failed model comparisons and photographic uncertainties are reported explicitly. The earlier version remains available through the record version history. We examine whether reproducible structural observations on the Phaistos Disc support a procedural interpretation. A pinned numerical transcription contains 242 main-sign positions, including one unreadable position, 45 readable sign types, 61 divider-defined groups and 18 supplementary stroke annotations. Source review reconciles counting and numbering conventions while retaining unresolved photographic uncertainty. The 02-to-12 side contrast persists after exact-family collapse. Adding side to a fixed position-only pairing predictor improves held-family loss by 0.082738 nats, but its exact conditional tail of 0.075 fails the frozen support rule. A positional mixture fails to outperform a bigram baseline. A separate directional test of the proposed 07-to-27 recovery relationship fails, with a one-sided permutation tail of 0.884. Supplementary-stroke comparisons have insufficient controlled overlap for the specified exact test. The work documents organization and constrains specific interpretations without establishing procedural functions or phonetic values. Corpus, code, protocols, full results and uncertainty ledgers accompany the paper.
items.title: Structural Organization and Interpretive Limits of the Phaistos Disc

items.summary: Large language models often penalize multilingual users through hidden 'tokenizer taxes' caused by subword fragmentation. Geographic proper nouns offer a controlled stress case for this distributional asymmetry, as they are standardized, cross-linguistically available entities whose orthographic forms frequently mismatch tokenizer training distributions. We introduce the Cross-Linguistic Orthographic Uniqueness Score (CLOUS), a character-level metric based on Shannon surprisal that quantifies the orthographic rarity of localized country names. We evaluate CLOUS on a controlled corpus of 249 ISO-registered country names; generalization to other geographic entity types remains future work. We evaluate CLOUS against tokenization fertility for six production tokenizers spanning three algorithm families across eleven languages and seven script families. Using Spearman rank correlation with Benjamini-Hochberg correction, CLOUS shows significant associative strength with fertility in 61 of 65 valid language-tokenizer combinations. As a screening tool for high-fragmentation entities, CLOUS achieves ROC-AUC = 0.850 and F1 = 0.740, correctly identifying approximately three-quarters of the highest-fragmentation entities from orthographic properties alone. We further show that CLOUS correlates with fertility more strongly than length-based baselines across all evaluated scripts, and outperforms a character bigram surprisal model in 69.2% of tested combinations, particularly for logographic, syllabic, and Latin scripts. Conversely, the bigram baseline proves superior for morphophonologically complex scripts like Arabic and Devanagari, indicating that tokenizer fragmentation is driven by local orthographic context in some scripts and absolute character rarity in others. Script family appears to be the primary driver of CLOUS-fertility correlation strength, with effect sizes ranging from modest for Latin-script languages ) to large for non-Latin scripts (   up to 0.686 for Japanese). These findings suggest that CLOUS may be useful as a lightweight pre-tokenization diagnostic for multilingual NLP pipelines.
items.title: Estimating Cross-Lingual Tokenization Fragmentation Risk: A Frequency-Based Uniqueness Score for Geographic Entities
